analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report the impacts of AI systems that decide who gets jobs, loans, housing, or care.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee for the rest of the Congress, with 15 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The Algorithmic Accountability Act would direct the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring large companies to study their own automated decision systems before and after using them. It covers systems that make 'critical decisions' about people — hiring, credit, housing, healthcare, insurance, education, and utilities. Companies would have to test whether those systems work differently for people of different races, sexes, ages, or incomes, document the data they train on, try to fix harms they find, file yearly reports with the FTC, and the FTC would publish a public, searchable record of who is using what kind of automated decision-making and how consumers can contest decisions. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose lives are increasingly shaped by software — applicants screened out of jobs by resume filters, renters and buyers scored by algorithms, patients whose care or coverage is steered by automated tools, and borrowers rated by models they never see. The bill would give them at least three things: a public FTC repository showing which companies use automated systems for which decisions and how to appeal one; testing requirements that measure whether a system performs worse for particular groups; and FTC or state attorney general enforcement when companies skip the work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered companies to perform impact assessments of automated decision systems both before and after deployment, including testing for differential performance by race, sex, age, disability, and other characteristics [S2].

Requires the FTC to build a publicly accessible, searchable repository showing which entities use which automated decision systems, what data they use, and how a consumer can contest, correct, or appeal a decision [S2].
Requires companies to attempt to eliminate or mitigate any likely material negative impact their systems have on consumers, and to document what they chose not to fix and why [S2].
Makes violations enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices and by state attorneys general on behalf of their residents, and expressly does not preempt stronger state or local laws [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large technology companies and any big firm that automates critical decisions — lenders, landlords, employers, insurers, healthcare systems, and the vendors that sell them AI tools. They would bear the cost of ongoing testing, documentation, stakeholder consultation, annual reporting to the FTC, and legal exposure from FTC and state enforcement. The bill applies only to larger entities (roughly those over $50 million in receipts or handling data on over 1 million people), leaving small businesses exempt [S2].

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be expensive: companies must maintain detailed documentation for years, consult outside stakeholders, and file recurring reports, and those costs would likely be passed on to consumers in some form [S2].

The bill requires companies to assess and report, but does not itself ban any practice; it caps staffing the FTC Bureau of Technology at 50 people plus 25 enforcement staff, so the whole scheme depends on an FTC with limited technical capacity writing rules within two years [S2].

Most of each impact assessment stays confidential — companies must file only a summary report with the FTC, and nothing in the bill creates a right for individuals to sue over violations, so a consumer harmed by an algorithm cannot take the company to court under this law [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that mandatory audits of every qualifying system could slow the deployment of beneficial automation, and the bill asks the FTC to weigh 'the administrative burden placed on the Commission and the covered entity' in its rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and growing problem: automated systems making consequential decisions about people with little transparency or recourse. Its design is transparency-first rather than prohibition-first, which is a genuine limitation — a company could document a biased system, file a summary report, and keep using it if it judged mitigation too costly. The compliance costs are real but fall only on large entities, and the public repository and state-enforcement provisions give consumers and regulators information they currently have no way to get. On balance, the benefits to ordinary people are larger than the costs, though the bill's reliance on a modest FTC staff is a real weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2023 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee, and no committee, subcommittee, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke (D-NY) introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 in the House on September 21, 2023 [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on September 22, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
That subcommittee referral was the bill's final action; it never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
The bill had 15 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large technology firms and other big companies that use automated decision systems are better off: no audit, documentation, reporting, or FTC enforcement regime was created, and their systems remain as opaque to consumers as before.

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 and recruited 15 Democratic cosponsors [S1].

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Robin Kelly, Emanuel Cleaver, Cori Bush, Pramila Jayapal, and Laurie Trahan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 15 were Democrats, with no Republican support [S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and committee majority of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full committee markup after its September 2023 referral; the subcommittee referral was the bill's last action for the rest of the Congress [S4].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor agenda throughout the bill's life and never brought it to a vote; no Republican cosponsored the bill [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans controlling the House, Energy and Commerce and the floor agenda, the bill never advanced beyond a subcommittee referral [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Large technology and AI software companies
industries.note: The bill would require them to test their automated decision systems for bias and harm, document their training data, file reports with the FTC, and appear in a public repository — ending the current practice of deploying such systems with no external visibility. Their interest in avoiding this runs against consumers' interest in transparency and recourse.

industries.industry: Data brokers and firms handling data on 1M+ consumers
industries.note: Entities meeting size or data-volume thresholds would become regulated 'covered entities' subject to assessments and annual FTC reporting, with a lower $5 million threshold for sellers of automated decision systems. This closes a gap in current law where algorithmic sellers face no disclosure duties.

industries.industry: Algorithm-driven lenders, landlords, employers, and insurers
industries.note: These industries would bear compliance costs for the screening and scoring tools they use on applicants and tenants, but clear rules and a public contest mechanism could reduce their exposure to discrimination claims and give them standards to follow.

industries.industry: AI compliance, auditing, and consulting services
industries.note: Mandatory impact assessments, independent auditing, and stakeholder consultation would create a market for algorithmic audit firms and compliance consultants serving covered entities.
